# OLTP vs OLAP

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/oltp_olap)

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## Definition
**Data warehousing** is a collection of **decision support**
technologies, aimed at enabling the **knowledge worker**
(executive, manager, analyst) to make better and faster
decisions.
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Even worse definition
A data warehouse is a "subject-oriented, integrated, time-
varying, non-volatile collection of data that is used primarily
in organizational decision making."
:::

Warehouses are **OLAP Gen 1**.

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/data_warehouse)


## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Data warehouse

- It is a separate database that analysts can query without affecting OLTP operations. 

- The data warehouse contains a read-only copy of the data in all the various OLTP systems in the company.
:::

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Extract–Transform–Load (ETL)

1. Data is extracted from OLTP databases (using either a periodic data dump or a continuous stream of updates)
2. transformed into an analysis-friendly schema
3. cleaned up 
4. and then loaded into the data warehouse. 
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## Why separate?

- trying to execute complex OLAP
queries against the operational databases would result in
unacceptable performance. 
- decision support requires non-OLTP data, such as **historical data**
- decision support requires consolidating data from many heterogeneous sources
- supporting the multidimensional data models and operations typical of
OLAP requires special data organization, access, and implementation methods
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Data warehouse rollout

1. define the architecture + capacity planning
2. integrate disparate servers
3. design schemas and views
4. connect data sources to the warehouse
5. define structure of physical storage
6. write scripts for ETL
7. implement end-user applications
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## ETL preparation: cleaning

- **data migration**: specify simple transformation rules
- **data scrubbing**: use domain-specific knowledge 
- **data auditing**: discover rules (or violations thereof) by scanning data
:::
    
## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Load preparation: preprocessing

- **checking integrity constraints**
- **sorting, summarization, aggregation, etc.**
- **indexing and building other access paths**
- **partitioning to multiple storage areas**
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## Commercial

- Microsoft SQL Server
- SAP HANA (**OLTAP**)
- Amazon RedShift
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Open-source

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## The divergence between OLTP DBs and data warehouses
Data warehouse:

- **Data model:** often relational
- **Query language:** often SQL-like
- **Internals:** quite different
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Dimensional model

- Multidimensional data model: a set of numeric **measures** that are the objects of analysis. 

- Each of the numeric measures depends on a set of **dimensions**

- A measure as a value in the multidimensional space of dimensions. 

- Each dimension is described by a set of **attributes**.
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/olap_dimensional_model)

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Star schema
The name “star schema” comes from the fact that when the table relationships are
visualized, the fact table is in the middle, surrounded by its dimension tables; the
connections to these tables are like the rays of a star.

- **fact table** -- collection of events occurring at particular time
- **dimension table** -- **who, what, where, when, how, and why** of the event.
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/star_schema_simple)

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/star_schema)

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Snowflake schema: definition
A variation of star schema, where dimensions are
further broken down into subdimensions. 

- more normalized than star schemas
- however, star schemas are often preferred because they are simpler for analysts to work with
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/snowflake_schema)

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## OLAP cubes
**Materialized aggregates:** data warehouse queries often involve an aggregate function, such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, or MAX in SQL. 

If the same aggregates are used often, they can be modified to be **materialized**.

**Relational model** offers **materialized views**.
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/olap_cube)


## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Operations

- **rollup**: increasing the level of aggregation 
- **drill-down**: decreasing the level of aggregation or increasing detail along one or more
dimension hierarchies
- **slice-and-dice**: selection and projection
- **pivot**: re-orienting the multidimensional view of data
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Pivoting
The simplest view of pivoting is that it selects two dimensions that are used to aggregate a measure.
:::

:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Rollup
Rollup corresponds to taking the current data object and
doing a further group-by on one of the dimensions. 

A converse is called **drill-down**.
:::

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Slice-and-dice
Slice-and-dice corresponds to
reducing the dimensionality of the data, i.e., taking a
projection of the data on a subset of dimensions for selected
values of the other dimensions.
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Data warehouse challenges

- couple compute and storage into an on-premises appliance. This forced enterprises to provision and pay for the peak of user load and data under management, which became very costly as datasets grew.
- more and more datasets were completely unstructured,
e.g., video, audio, and text documents, which data warehouses could
not store and query at all.
- **schema-on-write**
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Solution
**Data lakes** aka OLAP Gen 2.
Features:

- **schema-on-read**
- low-cost storage systems with a file API that hold data in generic and usually open file formats, such as Apache Parquet.
- data quality and governance: not solved
- hence downstream data warehouse (Teradata, AWS Redshift, Snowflake)
- 2-tier architecture
- started with HDFS (Apache Hadoop)
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Cloud data lake: storage layer

- Amazon S3
- ADLS (Microsoft)
- GCS (Google)
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/datalakes)

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Data lake issues

- **reliability**: keeping the data lake and warehouse consistent is
difficult and costly. There are subtle
differences between the data lake and warehouse engines.

- **data staleness**: the data in the warehouse is stale compared to that of the data lake. According to a survey by Dimensional Research and Fivetran, 86\% of analysts use out-of-date data and 62\% report waiting on engineering resources numerous times per month.

- **limited support for advanced analytics**: none of the leading ma- chine learning systems, such as TensorFlow, PyTorch and XGBoost, work well on top of warehouses. 

- **total cost of ownership**: users pay double the storage cost for data copied to a warehouse
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## Lakehouses
Compared to data warehouses:

- based on **open** direct-access data formats, such as Apache Parquet
- first-class support for **machine learning** and data science
- offer state-of-the-art **performance**.
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/lakehouses)

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Technologies enabling Lakehouse transition

- **Reliable data management on data lakes**: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg
- **Support for machine learning and data science:** Spark SQL
- **SQL performance:** Databricks Delta Engine, Presto, Trino
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Lakehouse definition
Lakehouse is a data management system based on low-cost and directly-accessible storage that also provides traditional analytical DBMS management and performance features such as:

- ACID transactions
- data versioning
- auditing
- indexing
- caching
- query optimization
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Lakehouse features

- **transactional metadata** layer on top of the object store that
defines **which** objects are part of a table version. 
- **SQL performances fixes:** caching, auxiliary data structures
such as indexes and statistics, and data layout optimizations
- **declarative DataFrame APIs:** TensorFlow and Spark MLlib
:::

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/lakehouses2)

## OLTP vs OLAP
![](img/datalake_tech_components)

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Lakehouses: Metadata
For instance, Apache Iceberg stores the information about which objects are part of a table in the data lake itself as a transaction log in Parquet format, enabling it to scale to billions of objects per table.
:::

![](img/presto)

## OLTP vs OLAP
:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Lakehouses: SQL

- give up data independence
- cache in SSD or RAM
- auxiliary data: statistics, Bloom filter for index, etc.
- data layout: order records by dimensions, or using space-filling curves (Z-order) and Hilbert curves
- whitebox compression
:::

:::{.callout-important icon=false}

# Columnar storage

## Columnar storage
:::{.callout-important icon=false}
## Problems

- fact tables are wide: **100+**, sometimes **hundreds** of columns
- typical OLAP queries access only **3-5** columns at a time
- but scan through **millions** of rows
:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Solution
Columnar storage to the rescue!

In OLTP databases, all values from a single **row** are stored together.

In columnar storage, all the values from a single **column** are stored together, instead.
:::
  
## Columnar storage
![](img/columnar_storage)

## Columnar storage
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## Vectorization

- efficient usage of CPU-memory bandwidth
- compress data so that it fits in CPU L1 cache
- SIMD
:::

## Columnar storage
:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## Sorting

- help with compression
- multiple sort orders
- slow down writes: solution is to use LSM trees
:::
